A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 326 327 Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 328 329 ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 330
331 {/* navigation links */} 332
333 ``` 334 335 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 336 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 337 animation: none; 338 z-index: 100; 339 } 340 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 341 display: none; 342 } 343 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 344 animation: none; 345 } 346 ``` 347 348 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The navigation triggers the transition; the `key={slug}` change makes React treat the old and new content as an exit/enter pair (activating `share`) instead of an in-place update. 416 417 If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states. 418 419 ## Next steps 420 421 You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. This convention is so ingrained that violating it feels disorienting. 219 220 Use the `transitionTypes` prop on `` to tag forward navigations: 221 222 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 223 224 {/* photo thumbnail */} 225 226 ``` 227 228 The same pattern works for any navigation within the app. For example, previous/next arrows on a photo detail page can use `nav-back` and `nav-forward` to animate in the corresponding direction. 229 230 For links that return the user to a previous page, use `nav-back`: 231 232 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 233 234 ← Gallery 235 236 ``` 237 238 The transition type is not automatic. You decide which links are "forward" and which are "back" based on your app's navigation hierarchy. 239 240 Then wrap page content in a `ViewTransition` that maps transition types to directional animations: 241 242 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 243 256 {/* page content */} 257 258 ``` 259 260 The `enter` and `exit` props accept an object keyed by transition type. When a navigation carries the `nav-forward` type, the exit animation slides old content left and the enter animation slides new content in from the right. The `default: "none"` ensures that transitions without a type (browser back/forward, `router.refresh()`, Suspense reveals) produce no directional animation. 261 262 Wrap every participating page the same way. For the gallery to slide out on forward navigation and back in on `nav-back`, its page needs the same wrapper. Put the wrapper in each `page.tsx`, not the layout. Layouts persist across navigations, so enter and exit never fire there: 263 264 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 265 278 279 280 ``` 281 282 The CSS for directional slides: 283 284 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 285 ::view-transition-old(.nav-forward) { 286 --slide-offset: -60px; 287 animation: 288 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 289 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 290 } 291 ::view-transition-new(.nav-forward) { 292 --slide-offset: 60px; 293 animation: 294 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 295 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 296 } 297 298 ::view-transition-old(.nav-back) { 299 --slide-offset: 60px; 300 animation: 301 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 302 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 303 } 304 ::view-transition-new(.nav-back) { 305 --slide-offset: -60px; 306 animation: 307 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 308 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 309 } 310 311 @keyframes slide { 312 from { 313 translate: var(--slide-offset); 314 } 315 to { 316 translate: 0; 317 } 318 } 319 ``` 320 321 The 60px offset is enough to communicate direction without making the user track a fast-moving element across the screen. 322 323 #### Anchoring the header 324 325 During directional slides, the header should not move. A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 326 327 Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 328 329 ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 330
331 {/* navigation links */} 332
333 ``` 334 335 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 336 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 337 animation: none; 338 z-index: 100; 339 } 340 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 341 display: none; 342 } 343 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 344 animation: none; 345 } 346 ``` 347 348 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `z-index: 100` ensures the header renders above the sliding content. 349 350 If we navigate forward to a photo, content slides left. If we click the "← Gallery" link (tagged with `nav-back`), content slides right. The header stays fixed throughout both transitions. 351 352 Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. The shared element morph from Step 1 still applies if both pages have matching `name` props. 353 354 #### Keeping the page interactive 355 356 While a transition runs, the `::view-transition` overlay captures pointer events, so clicks during the animation are lost. Let them pass through to the live page: 357 358 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 359 ::view-transition { 360 pointer-events: none; 361 } 362 ``` 363 364 This restores interactivity for unnamed content. Hit-testing still skips named participants (like the anchored header) for the transition's duration, so keep transitions short and avoid naming elements the user clicks rapidly. 365 366 #### Respecting reduced motion 367 368 Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 369 370 The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 371 372 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 373 @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 374 ::view-transition-old(*), 375 ::view-transition-new(*), 376 ::view-transition-group(*) { 377 animation-duration: 0s !important; 378 animation-delay: 0s !important; 379 } 380 } 381 ``` 382 383 Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. A more refined approach would preserve crossfades and opacity transitions while removing positional movement. See ["No Motion Isn't Always prefers-reduced-motion"](https://css-tricks.com/nuking-motion-with-prefers-reduced-motion/) for more on this. 384 385 ### Step 4: Crossfade content within the same route 386 387 The gallery has a photographer section with tabs. Each tab shows a different photographer's photos, but the route structure is the same: `/collection/[slug]`. Clicking between tabs does not feel like navigating to a new page. It feels like switching content within the same container. 388 389 A directional slide would be wrong here. Slides communicate "going to a new place." A crossfade communicates "same place, different content." The container persists (continuity), only the grid inside changes (swap). 390 391 Use a `ViewTransition` with `key` set to the current slug. When the key changes, React triggers a transition between the old and new content: 392 393 ```tsx filename="app/collection/[slug]/page.tsx" 394 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 395 396 export default async function CollectionPage({ params }) { 397 const { slug } = await params 398 399 return ( 400 }> 401 408 409 410 411 ) 412 } 413 ``` 414 415 The `share="auto"` and `enter="auto"` props tell React to use its default crossfade animation. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The navigation triggers the transition; the `key={slug}` change makes React treat the old and new content as an exit/enter pair (activating `share`) instead of an in-place update. 416 417 If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states. 418 419 ## Next steps 420 421 You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. Shared elements communicate continuity across routes. Suspense reveals animate loading handoffs. Directional slides encode navigation history. Crossfades signal content changes within the same location. 422 423 Each pattern answers a different question for the user: 424 425 | Pattern | What it communicates | 426 | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- | 427 | Shared element (morph) | "Same thing, going deeper" | 428 | Suspense reveal | "Data loaded" | 429 | Directional slide | "Going forward / coming back" | 430 | Same-route crossfade | "Same place, different content" | 431 432 For API details and more patterns: 433 434 - [Link `transitionTypes` prop](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#transitiontypes) 435 - [`useRouter`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-router), which also supports `transitionTypes` in `push()` and `replace()` 436 - [React `ViewTransition` component](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition) 437 - [Complete CSS from this guide](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo/blob/main/src/app/globals.css) — all keyframes and view transition rules in one file 438

Removing it from a diff only re-creates the uncommitted change; committing it with your work keeps the tree clean. 58 59 60 ``` 61 62 ## Using the codemod 63 64 To update to Next.js version 16, you can use the `upgrade` [codemod](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/codemods#160): 65 66 ```bash package="pnpm" 67 pnpm dlx @next/codemod@canary upgrade latest 68 ``` 69 70 ```bash package="npm" 71 npx @next/codemod@canary upgrade latest 72 ``` 73 74 ```bash package="yarn" 75 yarn dlx @next/codemod@canary upgrade latest 76 ``` 77 78 ```bash package="bun" 79 bunx @next/codemod@canary upgrade latest 80 ``` 81 82 The [codemod](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/codemods#160) is able to: 83 84 - Update `next.config.js` to use the new `turbopack` configuration 85 - Migrate from `next lint` to the ESLint CLI 86 - Migrate from deprecated `middleware` convention to `proxy` 87 - Remove `unstable_` prefix from stabilized APIs 88 - Remove `experimental_ppr` Route Segment Config from pages and layouts 89 90 The `upgrade` codemod does not run every migration codemod. If your app still uses synchronous `params`, `searchParams`, `cookies()`, `headers()`, or `draftMode()` access from the Next.js 15 compatibility period, also run the async Request APIs codemod: 91 92 ```bash filename="Terminal" 93 npx @next/codemod@canary next-async-request-api . 94 ``` 95 96 ## Install packages manually 97 98 If you prefer to do it manually, install the latest Next.js and React versions: 99 100 ```bash package="pnpm" 101 pnpm add next@latest react@latest react-dom@latest 102 ``` 103 104 ```bash package="npm" 105 npm install next@latest react@latest react-dom@latest 106 ``` 107 108 ```bash package="yarn" 109 yarn add next@latest react@latest react-dom@latest 110 ``` 111 112 ```bash package="bun" 113 bun add next@latest react@latest react-dom@latest 114 ``` 115 116 If you are using TypeScript, ensure you also upgrade `@types/react` and `@types/react-dom` to their latest versions. 117 118 ## Node.js runtime and browser support 119 120 | Requirement | Change / Details | 121 | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | 122 | Node.js 20.9+ | Minimum version now `20.9.0` (LTS); Node.js 18 no longer supported | 123 | TypeScript 5+ | Minimum version now `5.1.0` | 124 | Browsers | Chrome 111+, Edge 111+, Firefox 111+, Safari 16.4+ | 125 126 ## Turbopack by default 127 128 Starting with **Next.js 16**, Turbopack is stable and used by default with `next dev` and `next build` 129 130 Previously you had to enable Turbopack using `--turbopack`, or `--turbo`. 131 132 ```json filename="package.json" 133 { 134 "scripts": { 135 "dev": "next dev --turbopack", 136 "build": "next build --turbopack", 137 "start": "next start" 138 } 139 } 140 ``` 141 142 This is no longer necessary. You can update your `package.json` scripts: 143 144 ```json filename="package.json" 145 { 146 "scripts": { 147 "dev": "next dev", 148 "build": "next build", 149 "start": "next start" 150 } 151 } 152 ``` 153 154 If your project has a [custom `webpack`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/webpack) configuration and you run `next build` (which now uses Turbopack by default), the build will **fail** to prevent misconfiguration issues. 155 156 You have a few different ways to address this: 157 158 - **Use Turbopack anyway:** Run with `next build --turbopack` to build using Turbopack and ignore your `webpack` config. 159 - **Switch to Turbopack fully:** Migrate your `webpack` config to Turbopack-compatible options. 160 - **Keep using Webpack:** Use the `--webpack` flag to opt out of Turbopack and build with Webpack. 161 162 > **Good to know**: If you see failing builds because a `webpack` configuration was found, but you don't define one yourself, it is likely that a plugin is adding a `webpack` option 163 164 ### Opting out of Turbopack 165 166 If you need to continue using Webpack, you can opt out with the `--webpack` flag. For example, to use Turbopack in development but Webpack for production builds: 167 168 ```json filename="package.json" 169 { 170 "scripts": { 171 "dev": "next dev", 172 "build": "next build --webpack", 173 "start": "next start" 174 } 175 } 176 ``` 177 178 We recommend using Turbopack for development and production. Submit a comment to this [thread](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/77721), if you are unable to switch to Turbopack. 179 180 ### Turbopack configuration location 181 182 The `experimental.turbopack` configuration is out of experimental. 183 184 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 185 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 186 187 // Next.js 15 - experimental.turbopack 188 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 189 experimental: { 190 turbopack: { 191 // options 192 }, 193 }, 194 } 195 196 export default nextConfig 197 ``` 198 199 You can use it as a top-level `turbopack` option: 200 201 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 202 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 203 204 // Next.js 16 - turbopack at the top level of nextConfig 205 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 206 turbopack: { 207 // options 208 }, 209 } 210 211 export default nextConfig 212 ``` 213 214 Make sure to review the `Turbopack` configuration [options](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopack). **Next.js 16** introduces various improvements and new options, for example: 215 216 - [Advanced Webpack loader conditions](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopack#advanced-webpack-loader-conditions) 217 - [debugIds](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopack#debug-ids) 218 219 ### Resolve alias fallback 220 221 In some projects, client-side code may import files containing Node.js native modules. This will cause `Module not found: Can't resolve 'fs'` type of errors. 222 223 When this happens, you should refactor your code so that your client-side bundles do not reference these Node.js native modules. 224 225 However, in some cases, this might not be possible. In Webpack the `resolve.fallback` option was typically used to **silence** the error. Turbopack offers a similar option, using `turbopack.resolveAlias`. In this case, tell Turbopack to load an empty module when `fs` is requested for the browser. 226 227 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 228 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 229 230 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 231 turbopack: { 232 resolveAlias: { 233 fs: { 234 browser: './empty.ts', // We recommend to fix code imports before using this method 235 }, 236 }, 237 }, 238 } 239 240 export default nextConfig 241 ``` 242 243 It is preferable to refactor your modules so that client code doesn't ever import from modules using Node.js native modules. 244 245 ### Sass node_modules imports 246 247 Turbopack fully supports importing Sass files from `node_modules`. Note that while Webpack allowed the legacy tilde (`~`) prefix, Turbopack does not support this syntax. 248 249 In Webpack: 250 251 ```scss filename="styles/globals.scss" 252 @import '~bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css'; 253 ``` 254 255 In Turbopack: 256 257 ```scss filename="styles/globals.scss" 258 @import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css'; 259 ``` 260 261 If changing the imports is not possible, you can use `turbopack.resolveAlias`. For example: 262 263 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 264 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 265 266 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 267 turbopack: { 268 resolveAlias: { 269 '~*': '*', 270 }, 271 }, 272 } 273 274 export default nextConfig 275 ``` 276 277 ### Turbopack File System Caching 278 279 Turbopack stores compiler artifacts on disk between runs, for significantly faster compile times across restarts. Filesystem caching is enabled by default for both `next dev` and `next build`. See [`turbopackFileSystemCache`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackFileSystemCache) to configure or disable it. 280 281 ## Async Request APIs (Breaking change) 282 283 Version 15 introduced [Async Request APIs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-15#async-request-apis-breaking-change) as a breaking change, with **temporary** synchronous compatibility. 284 285 Starting with **Next.js 16**, synchronous access is fully removed. These APIs can only be accessed asynchronously. 286 287 - [`cookies`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cookies) 288 - [`headers`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/headers) 289 - [`draftMode`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/draft-mode) 290 - `params` in [`layout.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/layout), [`page.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), [`route.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route), [`default.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/default), [`opengraph-image`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/opengraph-image#opengraph-image), [`twitter-image`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/opengraph-image#twitter-image), [`icon`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/app-icons#icon), and [`apple-icon`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/app-icons#apple-icon). 291 - `searchParams` in [`page.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page) 292 293 Use the [codemod](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/codemods#migrate-to-async-dynamic-apis) to migrate to async Request-time APIs. 294 295 ### Migrating types for async Request-time APIs 296 297 To help migrate to async `params` and `searchParams`, you can run [`npx next typegen`](/docs/app/api-reference/cli/next#next-typegen-options) to automatically generate these globally available types helpers: 298 299 - [`PageProps`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#page-props-helper) 300 - [`LayoutProps`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/layout#layout-props-helper) 301 - [`RouteContext`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route#route-context-helper) 302 303 > **Good to know**: `typegen` was introduced in Next.js 15.5 304 305 This simplifies type-safe migration to the new async API pattern, and enables you to update your components with full type safety, for example: 306 307 ```tsx filename="/app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx" 308 export default async function Page(props: PageProps<'/blog/[slug]'>) { 309 const { slug } = await props.params 310 const query = await props.searchParams 311 return

Blog Post: {slug}

312 } 313 ``` 314 315 This approach gives you fully type-safe access to `props.params`, including the `slug`, and to `searchParams`, directly within your page. 316 317 ## Async parameters for icon, and open-graph Image (Breaking change) 318 319 > The props passed to the image generating functions in `opengraph-image`, `twitter-image`, `icon`, and `apple-icon`, are now Promises. 320 321 In previous versions, both the `Image` (image generation function), and the `generateImageMetadata` received a `params` object. The `id` returned by `generateImageMetadata` was passed as a string to the image generation function. 322 323 ```js filename="app/shop/[slug]/opengraph-image.js" 324 // Next.js 15 - synchronous params access 325 export function generateImageMetadata({ params }) { 326 const { slug } = params 327 return [{ id: '1' }, { id: '2' }] 328 } 329 330 // Next.js 15 - synchronous params and id access 331 export default function Image({ params, id }) { 332 const slug = params.slug 333 const imageId = id // string 334 // ... 335 } 336 ``` 337 338 Starting with **Next.js 16**, to align with the [Async Request APIs](#async-request-apis-breaking-change) change, the image generating function now receives `params` and `id` as promises. The `generateImageMetadata` function continues to receive synchronous `params`. 339 340 ```js filename="app/shop/[slug]/opengraph-image.js" 341 export async function generateImageMetadata({ params }) { 342 const { slug } = params 343 return [{ id: '1' }, { id: '2' }] 344 } 345 346 // Next.js 16 - asynchronous params and id access 347 export default async function Image({ params, id }) { 348 const { slug } = await params // params now async 349 const imageId = await id // id is now Promise when using generateImageMetadata 350 // ... 351 } 352 ``` 353 354 ## Async `id` parameter for `sitemap` (Breaking change) 355 356 Previously, the `id` values returned from [`generateSitemaps`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-sitemaps) were passed directly to the `sitemap` generating function. 357 358 ```js filename="app/product/sitemap.js" 359 export async function generateSitemaps() { 360 return [{ id: 0 }, { id: 1 }, { id: 2 }, { id: 3 }] 361 } 362 363 // Next.js 15 - synchronous id access 364 export default async function sitemap({ id }) { 365 const start = id * 50000 // id is a number 366 // ... 367 } 368 ``` 369 370 Starting with **Next.js 16**, the `sitemap` generating function now receives `id` as a promise. 371 372 ```js filename="app/product/sitemap.js" 373 export async function generateSitemaps() { 374 return [{ id: 0 }, { id: 1 }, { id: 2 }, { id: 3 }] 375 } 376 377 // Next.js 16 - asynchronous id access 378 export default async function sitemap({ id }) { 379 const resolvedId = await id // id is now Promise 380 const start = Number(resolvedId) * 50000 381 // ... 382 } 383 ``` 384 385 ## React 19.2 386 387 The App Router in **Next.js 16** uses the latest React [Canary release](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries), which includes the newly released React 19.2 features and other features being incrementally stabilized. Highlights include: 388 389 - **[View Transitions](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition)**: Animate elements that update inside a Transition or navigation 390 - **[`useEffectEvent`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffectEvent)**: Extract non-reactive logic from Effects into reusable Effect Event functions 391 - **[Activity](https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity)**: Render "background activity" by hiding UI with `display: none` while maintaining state and cleaning up Effects 392 393 Learn more in the [React 19.2 announcement](https://react.dev/blog/2025/10/01/react-19-2). 394 395 ## React Compiler Support 396 397 Built-in support for the React Compiler is now stable in **Next.js 16** following the React Compiler's 1.0 release. The React Compiler automatically memoizes components, reducing unnecessary re-renders with zero manual code changes. 398 399 The `reactCompiler` configuration option has been promoted from `experimental` to stable. It is not enabled by default as we continue gathering build performance data across different application types. 400 401 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 402 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 403 404 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 405 reactCompiler: true, 406 } 407 408 export default nextConfig 409 ``` 410 411 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 412 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 413 const nextConfig = { 414 reactCompiler: true, 415 } 416 417 module.exports = nextConfig 418 ``` 419 420 Install the latest version of the React Compiler plugin: 421 422 ```bash package="pnpm" 423 pnpm add -D babel-plugin-react-compiler 424 ``` 425 426 ```bash package="npm" 427 npm install -D babel-plugin-react-compiler 428 ``` 429 430 ```bash package="yarn" 431 yarn add -D babel-plugin-react-compiler 432 ``` 433 434 ```bash package="bun" 435 bun add -D babel-plugin-react-compiler 436 ``` 437 438 > **Good to know:** Expect compile times in development and during builds to be higher when enabling this option as the React Compiler relies on Babel. 439 440 ## Caching APIs 441 442 ### revalidateTag 443 444 [`revalidateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) now requires a second argument specifying a [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife#reference) profile. The single-argument form is deprecated and will produce a TypeScript error. 445 446 ```ts 447 // Before 448 revalidateTag('posts') 449 450 // After 451 revalidateTag('posts', 'max') 452 ``` 453 454 If you need immediate expiration rather than stale-while-revalidate, use [`updateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag) in Server Actions instead. 455 456 ```ts filename="app/actions.ts" switcher 457 'use server' 458 459 import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache' 460 461 export async function updateArticle(articleId: string) { 462 // Mark article data as stale - article readers see stale data while it revalidates 463 revalidateTag(`article-${articleId}`, 'max') 464 } 465 ``` 466 467 ```js filename="app/actions.js" switcher 468 'use server' 469 470 import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache' 471 472 export async function updateArticle(articleId) { 473 // Mark article data as stale - article readers see stale data while it revalidates 474 revalidateTag(`article-${articleId}`, 'max') 475 } 476 ``` 477 478 Use `revalidateTag` for content where a slight delay in updates is acceptable, such as blog posts, product catalogs, or documentation. Users receive stale content while fresh data loads in the background. 479 480 ### updateTag 481 482 [`updateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag) is a new [Server Actions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data#what-are-server-functions)-only API that provides **read-your-writes** semantics, where a user makes a change and the UI immediately shows the change, rather than stale data. 483 484 It does this by expiring and immediately refreshing data within the same request. 485 486 ```ts filename="app/actions.ts" switcher 487 'use server' 488 489 import { updateTag } from 'next/cache' 490 491 export async function updateUserProfile(userId: string, profile: Profile) { 492 await db.users.update(userId, profile) 493 494 // Expire cache and refresh immediately - user sees their changes right away 495 updateTag(`user-${userId}`) 496 } 497 ``` 498 499 ```js filename="app/actions.js" switcher 500 'use server' 501 502 import { updateTag } from 'next/cache' 503 504 export async function updateUserProfile(userId, profile) { 505 await db.users.update(userId, profile) 506 507 // Expire cache and refresh immediately - user sees their changes right away 508 updateTag(`user-${userId}`) 509 } 510 ``` 511 512 This ensures interactive features reflect changes immediately. Perfect for forms, user settings, and any workflow where users expect to see their updates instantly. 513 514 Learn more about when to use `updateTag` or `revalidateTag` [here](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag#when-to-use-updatetag). 515 516 ### refresh 517 518 [`refresh`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/refresh) allows you to refresh the client router from within a Server Action. 519 520 ```ts filename="app/actions.ts" switcher 521 'use server' 522 523 import { refresh } from 'next/cache' 524 525 export async function markNotificationAsRead(notificationId: string) { 526 // Update the notification in the database 527 await db.notifications.markAsRead(notificationId) 528 529 // Refresh the notification count displayed in the header 530 refresh() 531 } 532 ``` 533 534 ```js filename="app/actions.js" switcher 535 'use server' 536 537 import { refresh } from 'next/cache' 538 539 export async function markNotificationAsRead(notificationId) { 540 // Update the notification in the database 541 await db.notifications.markAsRead(notificationId) 542 543 // Refresh the notification count displayed in the header 544 refresh() 545 } 546 ``` 547 548 Use it when you need to refresh the client router after performing an action. 549 550 ### cacheLife and cacheTag 551 552 [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife) and [`cacheTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) are now stable. The `unstable_` prefix is no longer needed. 553 554 Wherever you had aliased imports like: 555 556 ```ts 557 import { 558 unstable_cacheLife as cacheLife, 559 unstable_cacheTag as cacheTag, 560 } from 'next/cache' 561 ``` 562 563 You can update your imports to: 564 565 ```ts 566 import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache' 567 ``` 568 569 ## Enhanced Routing and Navigation 570 571 **Next.js 16** includes a complete overhaul of the routing and navigation system, making page transitions leaner and faster. This optimizes how Next.js prefetches and caches navigation data: 572 573 - **Layout deduplication**: When prefetching multiple URLs with a shared layout, the layout is downloaded once. 574 - **Incremental prefetching**: Next.js only prefetches parts not already in cache, rather than entire pages. 575 576 These changes require **no code modifications** and are designed to improve performance across all apps. 577 578 However, you may see more individual prefetch requests with much lower total transfer sizes. We believe this is the right trade-off for nearly all applications. 579 580 If the increased request count causes issues, please let us know by creating an [issue](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues) or [discussion](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions) item. 581 582 ## Partial Prerendering (PPR) 583 584 **Next.js 16** removes the experimental **Partial Prerendering (PPR)** flag and configuration options, including the route level segment `experimental_ppr`. 585 586 Starting with **Next.js 16**, you can opt into PPR using the [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) configuration. 587 588 ```js filename="next.config.js" 589 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 590 const nextConfig = { 591 cacheComponents: true, 592 } 593 594 module.exports = nextConfig 595 ``` 596 597 PPR in **Next.js 16** works differently than in **Next.js 15** canaries. If you are using PPR today, stay in the current Next.js 15 canary you are using. See [Migrating to Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components) for migration patterns. 598 599 ```js filename="next.config.js" 600 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 601 const nextConfig = { 602 // If you are using PPR today 603 // stay in the current Next.js 15 canary 604 experimental: { 605 ppr: true, 606 }, 607 } 608 609 module.exports = nextConfig 610 ``` 611 612 ## `middleware` to `proxy` 613 614 The `middleware` filename is deprecated, and has been renamed to `proxy` to clarify network boundary and routing focus. 615 616 The `edge` runtime is **NOT** supported in `proxy`. The `proxy` runtime is `nodejs`, and it cannot be configured. If you want to continue using the `edge` runtime, keep using `middleware`. We will follow up on a minor release with further `edge` runtime instructions. 617 618 ```bash filename="Terminal" 619 # Rename your middleware file 620 mv middleware.ts proxy.ts 621 # or 622 mv middleware.js proxy.js 623 ``` 624 625 The named export `middleware` is also deprecated. Rename your function to `proxy`. 626 627 ```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher 628 export function proxy(request: Request) {} 629 ``` 630 631 ```js filename="proxy.js" switcher 632 export function proxy(request) {} 633 ``` 634 635 We recommend changing the function name to `proxy`, even if you are using a default export. 636 637 Configuration flags that contained the `middleware` name are also renamed. For example, `skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize` is now `skipProxyUrlNormalize` 638 639 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 640 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 641 642 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 643 skipProxyUrlNormalize: true, 644 } 645 646 export default nextConfig 647 ``` 648 649 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 650 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 651 const nextConfig = { 652 skipProxyUrlNormalize: true, 653 } 654 655 module.exports = nextConfig 656 ``` 657 658 The version 16 [codemod](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/codemods#160) is able to update these flags too. 659 660 ## `next/image` changes 661 662 ### Local Images with Query Strings (Breaking change) 663 664 Local image sources with query strings now require `images.localPatterns.search` configuration to prevent enumeration attacks. 665 666 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 667 import Image from 'next/image' 668 669 export default function Page() { 670 return 671 } 672 ``` 673 674 If you need to use query strings with local images, add the pattern to your configuration: 675 676 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 677 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 678 679 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 680 images: { 681 localPatterns: [ 682 { 683 pathname: '/assets/**', 684 search: '?v=1', 685 }, 686 ], 687 }, 688 } 689 690 export default nextConfig 691 ``` 692 693 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 694 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 695 const nextConfig = { 696 images: { 697 localPatterns: [ 698 { 699 pathname: '/assets/**', 700 search: '?v=1', 701 }, 702 ], 703 }, 704 } 705 706 module.exports = nextConfig 707 ``` 708 709 ### `minimumCacheTTL` Default (Breaking change) 710 711 The default value for `images.minimumCacheTTL` has changed from `60 seconds` to `4 hours` (14400 seconds). This reduces revalidation cost for images without cache-control headers. 712 713 For some Next.js users, image revalidation was happening frequently, often because the upstream source images missed a `cache-control` header. This caused revalidation to happen every `60` seconds, which increased CPU usage and cost. 714 715 Since most images do not change often, this short interval is not ideal. Setting the default to 4 hours offers a more durable cache by default, while still allowing images to update a few times per day if needed. 716 717 If you need the previous behavior, change `minimumCacheTTL` to a lower value, for example back to `60` seconds: 718 719 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 720 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 721 722 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 723 images: { 724 minimumCacheTTL: 60, 725 }, 726 } 727 728 export default nextConfig 729 ``` 730 731 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 732 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 733 const nextConfig = { 734 images: { 735 minimumCacheTTL: 60, 736 }, 737 } 738 739 module.exports = nextConfig 740 ``` 741 742 ### `imageSizes` Default (Breaking change) 743 744 The value `16` has been removed from the default `images.imageSizes` array. 745 746 We have looked at request analytics and found out that very few projects ever serve 16 pixels width images. Removing this setting reduces the size of the `srcset` attribute shipped to the browser by `next/image`. 747 748 If you need to support 16px images: 749 750 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 751 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 752 753 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 754 images: { 755 imageSizes: [16, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128, 256, 384], 756 }, 757 } 758 759 export default nextConfig 760 ``` 761 762 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 763 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 764 const nextConfig = { 765 images: { 766 imageSizes: [16, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128, 256, 384], 767 }, 768 } 769 770 module.exports = nextConfig 771 ``` 772 773 Rather than lack of developer usage, we believe 16 pixels width images have become less common, because `devicePixelRatio: 2` actually fetches a 32px image to prevent blurriness in retina displays. 774 775 ### `qualities` Default (Breaking change) 776 777 The default value for `images.qualities` has changed from allowing all qualities to only `[75]`. 778 779 If you need to support multiple quality levels: 780 781 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 782 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 783 784 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 785 images: { 786 qualities: [50, 75, 100], 787 }, 788 } 789 790 export default nextConfig 791 ``` 792 793 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 794 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 795 const nextConfig = { 796 images: { 797 qualities: [50, 75, 100], 798 }, 799 } 800 801 module.exports = nextConfig 802 ``` 803 804 If you specify a `quality` prop not included in the `image.qualities` array, the quality will be coerced to the closest value in `images.qualities`. For example, given the configuration above, a `quality` prop of 80, is coerced to 75. 805 806 ### Local IP Restriction (Breaking change) 807 808 A new security restriction blocks local IP optimization by default. Set `images.dangerouslyAllowLocalIP` to `true` only for private networks. 809 810 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 811 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 812 813 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 814 images: { 815 dangerouslyAllowLocalIP: true, // Only for private networks 816 }, 817 } 818 819 export default nextConfig 820 ``` 821 822 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 823 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 824 const nextConfig = { 825 images: { 826 dangerouslyAllowLocalIP: true, // Only for private networks 827 }, 828 } 829 830 module.exports = nextConfig 831 ``` 832 833 This might be necessary when hosting Next.js in a VPC with split-horizon DNS and you receive status 400 Bad Request. Only enable once you understand the SSRF risk. 834 835 ### Maximum Redirects (Breaking change) 836 837 The default for `images.maximumRedirects` has changed from unlimited to 3 redirects maximum. 838 839 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 840 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 841 842 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 843 images: { 844 maximumRedirects: 0, // Disable redirects 845 // or 846 maximumRedirects: 5, // Increase for edge cases 847 }, 848 } 849 850 export default nextConfig 851 ``` 852 853 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 854 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 855 const nextConfig = { 856 images: { 857 maximumRedirects: 0, // Disable redirects 858 // or 859 maximumRedirects: 5, // Increase for edge cases 860 }, 861 } 862 863 module.exports = nextConfig 864 ``` 865 866 ### `next/legacy/image` Component (deprecated) 867 868 The `next/legacy/image` component is deprecated. Use `next/image` instead: 869 870 ```tsx 871 // Before 872 import Image from 'next/legacy/image' 873 874 // After 875 import Image from 'next/image' 876 ``` 877 878 ### `images.domains` Configuration (deprecated) 879 880 The `images.domains` config is deprecated. 881 882 ```js filename="next.config.js" 883 // image.domains is deprecated 884 module.exports = { 885 images: { 886 domains: ['example.com'], 887 }, 888 } 889 ``` 890 891 Use `images.remotePatterns` instead for improved security: 892 893 ```js filename="next.config.js" 894 // Use image.remotePatterns instead 895 module.exports = { 896 images: { 897 remotePatterns: [ 898 { 899 protocol: 'https', 900 hostname: 'example.com', 901 }, 902 ], 903 }, 904 } 905 ``` 906 907 ## Concurrent `dev` and `build` 908 909 `next dev` and `next build` now use separate output directories, enabling concurrent execution. The `next dev` command outputs to `.next/dev`. 910 911 Additionally, a lockfile mechanism prevents multiple `next dev` or `next build` instances on the same project. 912 913 The [Turbopack tracing command](/docs/app/guides/local-development#turbopack-tracing) should be: 914 915 ```bash package="pnpm" 916 pnpm next internal trace .next-profiles/trace-turbopack.bin 917 ``` 918 919 ```bash package="npm" 920 npx next internal trace .next-profiles/trace-turbopack.bin 921 ``` 922 923 ```bash package="yarn" 924 yarn next internal trace .next-profiles/trace-turbopack.bin 925 ``` 926 927 ```bash package="bun" 928 bunx next internal trace .next-profiles/trace-turbopack.bin 929 ``` 930 931 ## Parallel Routes `default.js` requirement 932 933 All [parallel route](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/parallel-routes) slots now require explicit `default.js` files. Builds will fail without them. 934 935 To maintain previous behavior, create a [`default.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/default) file that calls `notFound()` or returns `null`. 936 937 ```tsx filename="app/@modal/default.tsx" 938 import { notFound } from 'next/navigation' 939 940 export default function Default() { 941 notFound() 942 } 943 ``` 944 945 Or return `null`: 946 947 ```tsx filename="app/@modal/default.tsx" 948 export default function Default() { 949 return null 950 } 951 ``` 952 953 ## ESLint Flat Config 954 955 `@next/eslint-plugin-next` now defaults to ESLint Flat Config format, aligning with ESLint v10 which will drop legacy config support. 956 957 Make sure to review our API reference for the [`@next/eslint-plugin-next`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/eslint#setup-eslint) plugin. 958 959 If you're using the legacy `.eslintrc` format, consider migrating to the flat config format. See the [ESLint migration guide](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/configure/migration-guide) for details. 960 961 ## Scroll Behavior Override 962 963 In **previous versions of Next.js**, if you had set `scroll-behavior: smooth` globally on your `` element via CSS, Next.js would override this during SPA route transitions, as follows: 964 965 1. Temporarily set `scroll-behavior` to `auto` 966 2. Perform the navigation (causing instant scroll to top) 967 3. Restore your original `scroll-behavior` value 968 969 This ensured that page navigation always felt snappy and instant, even when you had smooth scrolling enabled for in-page navigation. However, this manipulation could be expensive, especially at the start of every navigation. 970 971 In **Next.js 16**, this behavior has changed. By default, Next.js will **no longer override** your `scroll-behavior` setting during navigation. 972 973 **If you want Next.js to perform this override** (the previous default behavior), add the `data-scroll-behavior="smooth"` attribute to your `` element: 974 975 ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" 976 export default function RootLayout({ children }) { 977 return ( 978 979 {children} 980 981 ) 982 } 983 ``` 984 985 ## Performance Improvements 986 987 Significant performance optimizations for `next dev` and `next start` commands, along with improved terminal output with clearer formatting, better error messages, and improved performance metrics. 988 989 **Next.js 16** removes the `size` and `First Load JS` metrics from the `next build` output. We found these to be inaccurate in server-driven architectures using React Server Components. Both our Turbopack and Webpack implementations had issues, and disagreed on how to account for Client Components payload. 990 991 The most effective way to measure actual route performance is through tools such as [Chrome Lighthouse](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/overview) or Vercel Analytics, which focus on Core Web Vitals and downloaded resource sizes. 992 993 ### `next dev` config load 994 995 In previous versions the Next config file was loaded twice during development: 996 997 - When running the `next dev` command 998 - When the `next dev` command started the Next.js server 999 1000 This was inefficient because the `next dev` command doesn't need the config file to start the Next.js server. 1001 1002 A consequence of this change is that, when running `next dev` checking if `process.argv` includes `'dev'`, in your Next.js config file, will return `false`. 1003 1004 > **Good to know**: The `typegen`, and `build` commands, are still visible in `process.argv`. 1005 1006 This is specially important for plugins that trigger side-effects on `next dev`. If that's the case, it might be enough to check if `NODE_ENV` is set to `development`. 1007 1008 ```js filename="next.config.js" 1009 import { startServer } from 'docs-lib/dev-server' 1010 1011 const isDev = process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development' 1012 1013 if (isDev) { 1014 startServer() 1015 } 1016 1017 const nextConfig = { 1018 /* Your config options */ 1019 } 1020 1021 module.exports = nextConfig 1022 ``` 1023 1024 Alternatively, use the [`phase`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js#phase) in which the configuration is loaded. 1025 1026 ## Build Adapters API (alpha) 1027 1028 Following the [Build Adapters RFC](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/77740), the first alpha version of the Build Adapters API is now available. 1029 1030 Build Adapters allow you to create custom adapters that hook into the build process, enabling deployment platforms and custom build integrations to modify Next.js configuration or process build output. 1031 1032 ```js filename="next.config.js" 1033 const nextConfig = { 1034 experimental: { 1035 adapterPath: require.resolve('./my-adapter.js'), 1036 }, 1037 } 1038 1039 module.exports = nextConfig 1040 ``` 1041 1042 `adapterPath` was promoted to a stable, top-level option in 16.2.0. See [`adapterPath`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/adapterPath) for the current API reference. 1043 1044 ## Modern Sass API 1045 1046 `sass-loader` has been bumped to v16, which supports [modern Sass syntax](https://sass-lang.com/documentation/js-api/#md:usage) and new features. 1047 1048 ## Removals 1049 1050 These features were previously deprecated and are now removed: 1051 1052 ### AMP Support 1053 1054 AMP adoption has declined significantly, and maintaining this feature adds complexity to the framework. All AMP APIs and configurations have been removed: 1055 1056 - `amp` configuration from your Next config file 1057 - `next/amp` hook imports and usage (`useAmp`) 1058 1059 ```tsx 1060 // Removed 1061 import { useAmp } from 'next/amp' 1062 1063 // Removed 1064 export const config = { amp: true } 1065 ``` 1066 1067 - `export const config = { amp: true }` from pages 1068 1069 ```js filename="next.config.js" 1070 const nextConfig = { 1071 // Removed 1072 amp: { 1073 canonicalBase: 'https://example.com', 1074 }, 1075 } 1076 1077 export default nextConfig 1078 ``` 1079 1080 Evaluate if AMP is still necessary for your use case. Most performance benefits can now be achieved through Next.js's built-in optimizations and modern web standards. 1081 1082 ### `next lint` Command 1083 1084 The `next lint` command has been removed. Use Biome or ESLint directly. `next build` no longer runs linting. 1085 1086 A codemod is available to automate migration: 1087 1088 ```bash package="pnpm" 1089 pnpm dlx @next/codemod@canary next-lint-to-eslint-cli . 1090 ``` 1091 1092 ```bash package="npm" 1093 npx @next/codemod@canary next-lint-to-eslint-cli . 1094 ``` 1095 1096 ```bash package="yarn" 1097 yarn dlx @next/codemod@canary next-lint-to-eslint-cli . 1098 ``` 1099 1100 ```bash package="bun" 1101 bunx @next/codemod@canary next-lint-to-eslint-cli . 1102 ``` 1103 1104 The `eslint` option in the Next.js config file is also removed. 1105 1106 ```js filename="next.config.mjs" 1107 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 1108 const nextConfig = { 1109 // No longer supported 1110 // eslint: {}, 1111 } 1112 1113 export default nextConfig 1114 ``` 1115 1116 ### Runtime Configuration 1117 1118 `serverRuntimeConfig` and `publicRuntimeConfig` have been removed. Use environment variables instead. 1119 1120 **Before (Next.js 15):** 1121 1122 ```js filename="next.config.js" 1123 module.exports = { 1124 serverRuntimeConfig: { 1125 dbUrl: process.env.DATABASE_URL, 1126 }, 1127 publicRuntimeConfig: { 1128 apiUrl: '/api', 1129 }, 1130 } 1131 ``` 1132 1133 ```tsx filename="pages/index.tsx" 1134 import getConfig from 'next/config' 1135 1136 export default function Page() { 1137 const { publicRuntimeConfig } = getConfig() 1138 return

API URL: {publicRuntimeConfig.apiUrl}

1139 } 1140 ``` 1141 1142 **After (Next.js 16):** 1143 1144 For server-only values, access environment variables directly in Server Components: 1145 1146 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 1147 async function fetchData() { 1148 const dbUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL 1149 // Use for server-side operations only 1150 return await db.query(dbUrl, 'SELECT * FROM users') 1151 } 1152 1153 export default async function Page() { 1154 const data = await fetchData() 1155 return
{/* render data */}
1156 } 1157 ``` 1158 1159 > **Good to know**: Use the [taint API](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/taint) to prevent accidentally passing sensitive server values to Client Components. 1160 1161 For client-accessible values, use the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix: 1162 1163 ```bash filename=".env.local" 1164 NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL="/api" 1165 ``` 1166 1167 ```tsx filename="app/components/client-component.tsx" 1168 'use client' 1169 1170 export default function ClientComponent() { 1171 const apiUrl = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL 1172 return

API URL: {apiUrl}

1173 } 1174 ``` 1175 1176 To ensure environment variables are read at runtime (not bundled at build time), use the [`connection()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/connection) function before reading from `process.env`: 1177 1178 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 1179 import { connection } from 'next/server' 1180 1181 export default async function Page() { 1182 await connection() 1183 const config = process.env.RUNTIME_CONFIG 1184 return

{config}

1185 } 1186 ``` 1187 1188 Learn more about [environment variables](/docs/app/guides/environment-variables). 1189 1190 ### `devIndicators` Options 1191 1192 The following options have been removed from [`devIndicators`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/devIndicators): 1193 1194 - `appIsrStatus` 1195 - `buildActivity` 1196 - `buildActivityPosition` 1197 1198 The indicator itself remains available. 1199 1200 ### `experimental.dynamicIO` and `experimental.useCache` 1201 1202 The `experimental.dynamicIO` and `experimental.useCache` flags have been removed. 1203 1204 ```js filename="next.config.js" 1205 // Before: experimental.useCache 1206 module.exports = { 1207 experimental: { 1208 useCache: true, 1209 }, 1210 } 1211 ``` 1212 1213 ```js filename="next.config.js" 1214 // Before: experimental.dynamicIO 1215 module.exports = { 1216 experimental: { 1217 dynamicIO: true, 1218 }, 1219 } 1220 ``` 1221 1222 If you were actively using these flags, migrate to top-level [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents): 1223 1224 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 1225 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 1226 1227 // After 1228 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 1229 cacheComponents: true, 1230 } 1231 1232 export default nextConfig 1233 ``` 1234 1235 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 1236 // After 1237 module.exports = { 1238 cacheComponents: true, 1239 } 1240 ``` 1241 1242 If you were not actively adopting Cache Components, remove the flags instead. This reduces revalidation cost for images without cache-control headers. 712 713 For some Next.js users, image revalidation was happening frequently, often because the upstream source images missed a `cache-control` header. This caused revalidation to happen every `60` seconds, which increased CPU usage and cost. 714 715 Since most images do not change often, this short interval is not ideal. Use `next/image` instead: 869 870 ```tsx 871 // Before 872 import Image from 'next/legacy/image' 873 874 // After 875 import Image from 'next/image' 876 ``` 877 878 ### `images.domains` Configuration (deprecated) 879 880 The `images.domains` config is deprecated. 881 882 ```js filename="next.config.js" 883 // image.domains is deprecated 884 module.exports = { 885 images: { 886 domains: ['example.com'], 887 }, 888 } 889 ``` 890 891 Use `images.remotePatterns` instead for improved security: 892 893 ```js filename="next.config.js" 894 // Use image.remotePatterns instead 895 module.exports = { 896 images: { 897 remotePatterns: [ 898 { 899 protocol: 'https', 900 hostname: 'example.com', 901 }, 902 ], 903 }, 904 } 905 ``` 906 907 ## Concurrent `dev` and `build` 908 909 `next dev` and `next build` now use separate output directories, enabling concurrent execution. The `next dev` command outputs to `.next/dev`. 910 911 Additionally, a lockfile mechanism prevents multiple `next dev` or `next build` instances on the same project. 912 913 The [Turbopack tracing command](/docs/app/guides/local-development#turbopack-tracing) should be: 914 915 ```bash package="pnpm" 916 pnpm next internal trace .next-profiles/trace-turbopack.bin 917 ``` 918 919 ```bash package="npm" 920 npx next internal trace .next-profiles/trace-turbopack.bin 921 ``` 922 923 ```bash package="yarn" 924 yarn next internal trace .next-profiles/trace-turbopack.bin 925 ``` 926 927 ```bash package="bun" 928 bunx next internal trace .next-profiles/trace-turbopack.bin 929 ``` 930 931 ## Parallel Routes `default.js` requirement 932 933 All [parallel route](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/parallel-routes) slots now require explicit `default.js` files. Builds will fail without them. 934 935 To maintain previous behavior, create a [`default.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/default) file that calls `notFound()` or returns `null`. 936 937 ```tsx filename="app/@modal/default.tsx" 938 import { notFound } from 'next/navigation' 939 940 export default function Default() { 941 notFound() 942 } 943 ``` 944 945 Or return `null`: 946 947 ```tsx filename="app/@modal/default.tsx" 948 export default function Default() { 949 return null 950 } 951 ``` 952 953 ## ESLint Flat Config 954 955 `@next/eslint-plugin-next` now defaults to ESLint Flat Config format, aligning with ESLint v10 which will drop legacy config support. 956 957 Make sure to review our API reference for the [`@next/eslint-plugin-next`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/eslint#setup-eslint) plugin. 958 959 If you're using the legacy `.eslintrc` format, consider migrating to the flat config format. See the [ESLint migration guide](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/configure/migration-guide) for details. 960 961 ## Scroll Behavior Override 962 963 In **previous versions of Next.js**, if you had set `scroll-behavior: smooth` globally on your `` element via CSS, Next.js would override this during SPA route transitions, as follows: 964 965 1. Temporarily set `scroll-behavior` to `auto` 966 2. Perform the navigation (causing instant scroll to top) 967 3. Restore your original `scroll-behavior` value 968 969 This ensured that page navigation always felt snappy and instant, even when you had smooth scrolling enabled for in-page navigation. Both our Turbopack and Webpack implementations had issues, and disagreed on how to account for Client Components payload. 990 991 The most effective way to measure actual route performance is through tools such as [Chrome Lighthouse](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/overview) or Vercel Analytics, which focus on Core Web Vitals and downloaded resource sizes. 992 993 ### `next dev` config load 994 995 In previous versions the Next config file was loaded twice during development: 996 997 - When running the `next dev` command 998 - When the `next dev` command started the Next.js server 999 1000 This was inefficient because the `next dev` command doesn't need the config file to start the Next.js server. 1001 1002 A consequence of this change is that, when running `next dev` checking if `process.argv` includes `'dev'`, in your Next.js config file, will return `false`. 1003 1004 > **Good to know**: The `typegen`, and `build` commands, are still visible in `process.argv`. 1005 1006 This is specially important for plugins that trigger side-effects on `next dev`. See [`adapterPath`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/adapterPath) for the current API reference. 1043 1044 ## Modern Sass API 1045 1046 `sass-loader` has been bumped to v16, which supports [modern Sass syntax](https://sass-lang.com/documentation/js-api/#md:usage) and new features. 1047 1048 ## Removals 1049 1050 These features were previously deprecated and are now removed: 1051 1052 ### AMP Support 1053 1054 AMP adoption has declined significantly, and maintaining this feature adds complexity to the framework. All AMP APIs and configurations have been removed: 1055 1056 - `amp` configuration from your Next config file 1057 - `next/amp` hook imports and usage (`useAmp`) 1058 1059 ```tsx 1060 // Removed 1061 import { useAmp } from 'next/amp' 1062 1063 // Removed 1064 export const config = { amp: true } 1065 ``` 1066 1067 - `export const config = { amp: true }` from pages 1068 1069 ```js filename="next.config.js" 1070 const nextConfig = { 1071 // Removed 1072 amp: { 1073 canonicalBase: 'https://example.com', 1074 }, 1075 } 1076 1077 export default nextConfig 1078 ``` 1079 1080 Evaluate if AMP is still necessary for your use case. Most performance benefits can now be achieved through Next.js's built-in optimizations and modern web standards. 1081 1082 ### `next lint` Command 1083 1084 The `next lint` command has been removed. Use Biome or ESLint directly. `next build` no longer runs linting. 1085 1086 A codemod is available to automate migration: 1087 1088 ```bash package="pnpm" 1089 pnpm dlx @next/codemod@canary next-lint-to-eslint-cli . 1090 ``` 1091 1092 ```bash package="npm" 1093 npx @next/codemod@canary next-lint-to-eslint-cli . 1094 ``` 1095 1096 ```bash package="yarn" 1097 yarn dlx @next/codemod@canary next-lint-to-eslint-cli . 1098 ``` 1099 1100 ```bash package="bun" 1101 bunx @next/codemod@canary next-lint-to-eslint-cli . 1102 ``` 1103 1104 The `eslint` option in the Next.js config file is also removed. 1105 1106 ```js filename="next.config.mjs" 1107 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 1108 const nextConfig = { 1109 // No longer supported 1110 // eslint: {}, 1111 } 1112 1113 export default nextConfig 1114 ``` 1115 1116 ### Runtime Configuration 1117 1118 `serverRuntimeConfig` and `publicRuntimeConfig` have been removed. 1139 } 1140 ``` 1141 1142 **After (Next.js 16):** 1143 1144 For server-only values, access environment variables directly in Server Components: 1145 1146 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 1147 async function fetchData() { 1148 const dbUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL 1149 // Use for server-side operations only 1150 return await db.query(dbUrl, 'SELECT * FROM users') 1151 } 1152 1153 export default async function Page() { 1154 const data = await fetchData() 1155 return
